then.text: Two points of light hang in the sea-fog on the clifftop, steady as lamps. They are looking at you.

else.text: A great bank of fog rolls up over the abbey ruins in a minute and a half. Out of it, on four huge silent paws, steps a black dog the size of a pony.
Its eyes are two lamps. Its coat doesn't so much shine as absorb the light from around it. A herring gull on the wall, who has seen everything, takes a step sideways.
Do not be afraid. Everyone is, at first. It's the size, I think. And the eyes. And the way I tend to turn up at the end of a bad night.
I came ashore from a wrecked ship in a story, and the story gave me a very good press agent. I've just been walking this cliff ever since, being looked at.
They say a person who sees me will not see the year out. This is nonsense. I merely walk people home. It's usually a long way and quite a lot of steps. A hundred and ninety-nine, in fact. Shall we?

then.text: The great black dog pads to your side and sits, enormous and unhurried, with its eyes like two lamps turned down low. Down the cliff, a gull screams at it. It does not look round. The gull finds a lamp-post to be somewhere else on.

else.text: Black Shuck steps backwards into the fog that has, without anybody noticing, arrived, and is gone. Somewhere on the cliff path, one slow bark. You are fairly sure it said 'next time'.
On the clifftop above the abbey, something large and black sits against the sky, as still as a statue. When you look straight at it, it's a gatepost. When you look away, it has ears.
Not yet, little walker. I only keep company with those who carry all ten. You have nine, and a very good start.
The fog comes in from the sea, wraps the clifftop for a moment, and goes out again. The gatepost is a gatepost. Probably.

rail_guard.text: Whitby Station. The end of the line, quite literally, or the start of it, depending on whether you have a bag of chips.
All aboard! The trains go everywhere you have been. Mind the gap, and the herring gull.

wby_chipper.text: Haddock, chips, mushy peas, bread and butter, and a pot of tea. Yorkshire law, that is. The haddock is from the boat you just saw.
Watch your chips. The gulls here are professionals. They don't dive. They wait until you look at the sea.

then.text: Mind the dust, love. And mind your Jetling, if you've got one. A little polish and it'll gleam like a good intention.
Whitby jet is patience, the old carvers say. Ten years to learn to carve a rose. Twenty to stop being annoyed by it.

else.text: Whitby jet is fossilised monkey-puzzle wood, nearly 180 million years old. You can carve it, and it takes a lovely polish, and it will pull a tiny scrap of paper to itself if you rub it.
Queen Victoria wore it in mourning, so every lady in the land wanted it. At the peak there were two hundred jet workshops in this little town. Now there are some. I'm one.
The jet carver holds out a polishing cloth. Try your hand at a piece?

then.text: Light hands, love. Small circles. Think of it as stroking a cat who is a bit shy of you.

Well, now. That's not bad at all. You've the touch. There's a glow on it you won't get from a shop. Here, keep it. It's good for a Jetling, if you've got one, and for the look of the thing if you haven't.

else.text: Another time, then. The jet'll wait. It's waited a hundred and eighty million years. It's very good at it.

then.text: Fog on the abbey! This is exactly the weather I dressed for. I have never been happier.
Sunshine. Hmm. My velvet wasn't made for this. I'll be in the shade by the bandstand.
Dusk on the 199 steps, bats out over the abbey. Perfect. Absolutely perfect.

wby_goth.text: Whitby Goth Weekend! Twice a year, thousands of us arrive in black velvet and top hats and walk up the 199 steps, because that is what Dracula would do.
The locals are delighted. A top hat on a Goth is a statement. A seagull wearing it is a different matter.

then.text: Gale blowing in off the North Sea. Nobody's sailing today. Not even Captain Cook would.
Sea fret coming in. That's what we call fog off the sea round here. Thick as soup.
Bit of rain on the harbour. The boats don't mind, they're wet on the bottom anyway.

wby_skipper.text: The Endeavour was built here in 1764 as a coal ship called the Earl of Pembroke. The navy bought it, renamed it, and sent Captain Cook round the world in it. A Whitby collier, circling the globe!
Colliers were broad and flat-bottomed, so they could sit on the mud at low tide without falling over. A good ship for the unknown.

then.text: Fog on the cliffs, gulls in the grey. I feel a poem coming on. Probably a limerick.
This wind keeps stealing my poems. Somewhere in Scarborough someone's reading my best work.

wby_bard.text: Caedmon was a cowherd who was too shy to sing at feasts. He left one night, had a dream, and woke up able to sing in his own language. He sang, in English, about creation. It's the oldest English poem we have.
I have written nine hundred poems and a limerick. The limerick is the one people remember.
